title: A Circuit for In-Context Learning
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) lets a pretrained language model perform a task specified by demonstrations in its prompt, with no parameter updates. With arbitrary labels the model must acquire a mapping it cannot have memorized, so the learning happens within a single forward pass. Prior work found candidate parts but not how they compose. We give the composition for few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B-parameter transformers. The model implements a key-value memory over label-token positions: each label token's residual stream encodes the label's identity, and middle-layer attention heads write into it the class of the preceding demonstration as its key. At the query, upper-layer heads match the query's class against the stored keys and copy out the matching labels. An early-layer signal encoding whether any label has repeated gates this readout; in its absence the readers attend to the start of the prompt and no label is favored. A separate set of heads suppresses the most recently seen label. Each step is established causally by activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the model's own signals. A softmax model of the readout with two constants per head, fit on one prompt distribution, predicts another. The computation is conserved across the three models, the named heads alone reproduce the behaviour, and a transformer trained from scratch grows the same parts. The circuit transfers to semantic concepts and to labels with meaning, and the same parts, with a causal gate, appear from 0.6B to 8B in one family and survive instruction tuning. ICL in this setting is a gated associative lookup built from a few identifiable component types, traced causally from demonstrations to prediction.
approach: Mechanistic circuit analysis of few-shot sentence classification with arbitrary labels in three 3-4B transformers: activation patching, head ablations against random-head baselines, and steering with the models' own signals, plus a two-constant-per-head softmax readout model fit on one prompt distribution and tested on another.
finding: ICL is a gated associative lookup. Middle-layer heads write the preceding demonstration's class as a key into label-token residual streams; upper-layer heads match the query's class to those keys and copy out the labels. An early-layer 'any label repeated' signal gates the readout (without it, readers default to the prompt start), and a separate head group suppresses the most recently seen label. The circuit is conserved across three models, reproduced from the named heads alone, emerges in a transformer trained from scratch, and persists from 0.6B to 8B and through instruction tuning.
note: arXiv preprint — not peer reviewed. The explicit label-position KV write and recency-suppression heads are the most concrete circuit-level statement yet of Pillar 1/3 address-and-readout structure.

title: Where Should a KV-Cache Repair Budget Go? Distractor Structure and Contextual Compatibility in Non-Prefix Reuse
abstract: Non-prefix KV-cache reuse encodes retrieved chunks independently and concatenates their caches. To find where a small repair budget should be spent, we vary the chunks around the answer-bearing one (the target) across three 7B-8B models and four datasets of dialogue memory, open-domain QA and API documentation. Reuse loses 19-100% of the context-dependent questions that full prefill answers, and it loses more when the other chunks are of the same kind as the target. Because the recoverable damage is spread over these other chunks, restoring a few of them recovers little, and the budget is better spent on the target. This works through contextual compatibility: recomputing the target against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven settings tested, although the recomputed KV stays far from the full-prefill KV. Question attention over reused caches, however, selects the target in at most 18.8% of development questions. A retriever finds it more often, and recomputing its top chunk after moving it next to the question significantly beats InfoFlow-style reordering at the same 5% budget in six of nine open-domain QA and API-documentation settings. On dialogue memory, though, recomputing chunks never significantly beats the token-level selector chosen for each setting.
approach: Controlled manipulation of the chunks surrounding the answer-bearing target under non-prefix KV-cache reuse across three 7B-8B models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B) and four datasets (LoCoMo dialogue memory, NQ-Open, TriviaQA, Gorilla); scoring only questions full prefill answers that require retrieved context, with a 5% recomputation budget.
finding: Reuse loses 19-100% of context-dependent questions, and similarity-matched distractors make it significantly worse (9/12 settings). Recoverable damage is spread over distractors, so the budget belongs on the target: recomputing the target against the reused cache beats inserting its full-prefill KV in all seven settings even though the recomputed KV stays 0.23-0.30 relative distance away — what matters is encoding consistency, not approaching reference values. Question attention identifies the target in at most 18.8% of cases; moving the retriever's top chunk adjacent to the question and recomputing it beats reordering in 6/9 settings, but the effect does not transfer to dialogue memory.
note: arXiv preprint — not peer reviewed. 'Contextual compatibility' is a mechanistic account of why a stored KV is not portable: a value must be encoded in the presence of its neighbours.

title: Muir: Linear Attention with Sensitivity-Allocated Gating and Matched-Filter Readout
authors: Tushaar Gangavarapu et al. (Clemens J. S. Schaefer)
abstract: Linear attention compresses context into a fixed-size key-value state for linear-time training and constant-memory inference. Gated delta-rule models decay this state and erase its prediction for an incoming key before writing a new value; Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2) generalizes this with channel-wise decay and decoupled, full-rank erase and write gates. However, we show that state updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes: key activation and unit normalization concentrate key energy onto a sparse subset of channels, whereas value writes scale all channels, so the erase gate can be parameterized at lower rank. Furthermore, slow-decaying state rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Guided by this analysis, we introduce Muir, which fuses all gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weights state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvests the saved parameters in a wider feed-forward network. Because standard chunkwise algorithms become numerically unstable at the large chunk sizes needed to saturate wide matrix units, we design a parallel update for stable, efficient training. Across 166M-1.34B parameters, Muir lowers perplexity by 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy by up to 1.9 points, and improves extractive recall over GDN-2. At 1.34B, Muir outperforms both baselines on multi-hop and multi-needle recall, extrapolates 2,560x from its 4K training length to 10M-token streams without perplexity drift, and maintains near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens with static readout. Muir achieves these gains while matching GDN-2 throughput, reaching its 100B-token validation loss 1.2x faster, and training 2.7x faster than Transformer at 32K.
approach: Sensitivity analysis of gated delta-rule linear-attention states (166M-1.34B parameters) followed by an architecture change: fuse erase/write gates into a sensitivity-allocated low-rank projection, re-weight state rows with a matched-filter readout gate, and reinvest saved parameters in a wider FFN; a parallel update is derived because chunkwise algorithms become unstable at large chunk sizes.
finding: State updates are far less sensitive to erasure than to writes — key energy concentrates on a sparse channel subset while value writes scale all channels — and slow-decaying rows accumulate much larger norms than fast rows, dominating unweighted readout and forcing stronger write-time erasure to suppress interference. Re-weighting the readout by those norms lowers perplexity 1.8-2.0% over GDN-2 and 2.5-3.6% over Transformer, raises commonsense accuracy up to 1.9 points, extrapolates 2,560x from 4K training to 10M-token streams with no perplexity drift, and holds near-100% passkey retrieval to 1M tokens.
note: arXiv preprint — not peer reviewed. The write/erase asymmetry and row-norm interference are the same objects as the KV state-decay questions in Pillar 3.

title: Persistent hippocampal traces of lifelong spatial memory
authors: J. Wu et al. (M. Meister, C. Lois)
abstract: Memory presents a biological paradox: the brain changes continuously, yet a brief experience can influence behavior for a lifetime. How such memories are stored in brain circuits remains unclear. Here we show that two days in a binary-tree maze leave mice with spatial memories that survive repeated 90-day absences over as much as a year. Across return visits, mice explored the maze more efficiently than when naive and resumed direct runs to a reward location sooner, both by a factor of 3. Chronic calcium imaging of the same hippocampal CA1 neurons showed that although most neurons had changed their preferred locations, the population activity at a given maze location still resembled the pattern from 90 days earlier. Furthermore, even when a neuron's place fields changed location, they tended to remain at the same branching level of the binary tree, reflecting the local geometry of the maze. In return sessions where the neural tuning for branching level was preserved more accurately, the mouse explored the environment more efficiently. Population patterns were best preserved near the reward location, and more reliable neural activity there accompanied earlier direct runs to the reward. With repeated experience, spatial representations changed less, both within a visit and across the long absences. A brief experience thus left selective hippocampal traces that survived months of absence despite drift, grew more durable with each return, and were correlated with memory in navigation behavior.
approach: Mice spent two days in a binary-tree maze, then returned after repeated 90-day absences over as much as a year; chronic calcium imaging tracked the same CA1 neurons across visits while navigation efficiency and direct runs to the reward were measured.
finding: Spatial memory survived up to a year: return visits were ~3x more efficient than naive exploration and direct reward runs resumed ~3x sooner. Although most neurons changed preferred locations, the population pattern at a given location still resembled the one 90 days earlier, and cells whose fields moved tended to stay at the same branching level of the maze. Sessions with better-preserved branching-level tuning were explored more efficiently, and patterns were best preserved near reward. Representations changed less with each repeated experience.
note: Preprint, not peer reviewed. DOI stem is 10-30 but the bioRxiv API posting date is 11-06. A rare direct measurement of what survives representational drift: abstract topological position, not the place field.

title: Hippocampal transformations occur along dimensions of memory interference
authors: Soroush Mirjalili et al. (Brice A. Kuhl)
abstract: Abstract The role of the hippocampus in resolving memory interference has been greatly elucidated by considering the relationship between the similarity of visual stimuli (input) and corresponding similarity of hippocampal activity patterns (output). However, these input-output functions can take surprisingly different forms. Here, we reconcile seemingly conflicting findings by considering the possibility that the hippocampus prioritizes different dimensions of visual similarity across different stages of learning. First, we generated a set of natural scene images from two visual categories and rigorously characterized visual similarity using a wide array of methods: neural networks, artificial intelligence models, and human perceptual and memory decisions. We then identified two orthogonal dimensions of visual similarity that each predicted memory interference, but that did so at distinct stages of learning. Using high-resolution fMRI, we then tested for dimension-specific input-output functions within the hippocampus. Within CA3 and dentate gyrus (CA3/DG), we show that dimensions of visual similarity were inverted (repulsion) at stages of learning when they contributed to memory interference. In contrast, CA3/DG preserved similarity when dimensions did not contribute to interference. These findings reveal that hippocampal representations of visually-similar stimuli are highly dynamic and critically depend on the dimensions of similarity that currently contribute to memory interference.
approach: Generated natural-scene images from two categories and characterised visual similarity with neural-network/AI models plus human perceptual and memory judgments, isolating two orthogonal similarity dimensions; then used high-resolution fMRI to measure dimension-specific input-output functions in hippocampus across stages of learning.
finding: The two visual-similarity dimensions each predicted memory interference, but at different learning stages. Within CA3/dentate gyrus, similarity was inverted (repulsion) exactly on the dimension currently contributing to interference, and preserved on the dimension that was not. Hippocampal representations of similar stimuli are therefore dynamic and re-weighted by whichever similarity axis is behaviourally costly at that moment.
note: Reconciles competing 'pattern separation vs completion' findings by making the transformation conditional on the interference dimension — directly relevant to schema-guided remapping.

title: Circuit regulation along an activity continuum shapes flexible and stable representations during learning
abstract: Learning requires neural representations to flexibly incorporate new information while progressively stabilizing to support enduring memories. How neural circuits balance these demands remains unclear. Here, we identify complementary mechanisms supporting representational flexibility and stability in the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), a key component of the cognitive map for memory-guided navigation. Longitudinal calcium imaging in mice learning novel virtual environments revealed a persistent axis of excitatory neuronal activity associated with distinct representational dynamics. Low-activity neurons exhibited intermittent activation that varied with learning stages and greater learning-dependent representational refinement, flexibly shifting their encoding from landmarks toward reward locations. By contrast, high-activity neurons exhibited more persistent activation and maintained more stable spatial representations. Dopaminergic pre-reward ramping was associated with the emergence of reward encoding in low-activity neurons, whereas interactions with inhibitory interneurons contributed to the stability of high-activity neurons. Notably, interneurons exhibited activity changes opposing those of excitatory neurons during learning, and their transient activation upon novelty exposure delayed excitatory representational remodeling, stabilization, and behavioral learning, suggesting that inhibitory circuits gate learning-dependent representational dynamics. Together, these findings reveal how activity-dependent excitatory neuronal organization and circuit-level regulation enable complementary forms of representational flexibility and stability to coexist, facilitating the incorporation of novel experiences into stable, context-specific cognitive maps that support learning.
approach: Longitudinal two-photon calcium imaging of medial entorhinal cortex in mice learning novel virtual environments, combined with dopaminergic recordings, interneuron manipulation, and behavioural learning measures.
finding: A persistent axis of excitatory activity predicts representational fate: low-activity neurons activate intermittently, refine strongly with learning, and shift encoding from landmarks toward reward (with dopaminergic pre-reward ramping predicting the shift), while high-activity neurons fire persistently and hold stable spatial maps. Interneurons change in the opposite direction, and transiently activating them on novelty exposure delays excitatory remapping, stabilisation and behavioural learning — i.e. inhibition gates how fast a cognitive map is rewritten.
note: Preprint, not peer reviewed. DOI stem 10-28; bioRxiv API posting date 11-03. A circuit-level answer to the stability/plasticity trade-off in the same structure TCM-style context drift lives in.

title: Redundancy maximization as a principle of associative memory learning in Hopfield networks
abstract: Abstract Associative memory, traditionally modeled by Hopfield networks, enables the retrieval of previously stored patterns from partial or noisy cues. Yet, the local computational principles which are required to enable this function remain incompletely understood. To formally characterize the local information processing in such systems, we employ a recent extension of information theory—Partial Information Decomposition. It decomposes the contribution of different inputs to an output into unique information from each input, redundant information across inputs, and synergistic information that emerges from combining different inputs. Applying this framework to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks we find that below the memory capacity, the information in a neuron’s activity is characterized by high redundancy between the external pattern input and the internal recurrent input, while synergy and unique information are close to zero until the memory capacity is surpassed and performance drops steeply. Inspired by this observation, we use redundancy maximization at each neuron as an information-theoretic learning goal. This increases the network’s memory capacity to 1.59, a more than tenfold improvement over the 0.14 capacity of classical Hopfield networks, and also outperforming recent state-of-the-art implementations of Hopfield networks. Overall, this work establishes redundancy maximization as a design principle for associative memories and opens pathways for new associative memory models based on information-theoretic goals.
approach: Applied Partial Information Decomposition to individual neurons in classical Hopfield networks, decomposing each unit's information into unique, redundant and synergistic contributions from external pattern input versus internal recurrent input; then used redundancy maximisation at each neuron as a local learning objective.
finding: Below memory capacity, a neuron's activity is dominated by redundancy between the external pattern and the recurrent input, while synergy and unique information stay near zero — until capacity is exceeded and performance collapses. Training each neuron to maximise that redundancy raises capacity from 0.14 to 1.59, a >10-fold gain that also beats recent state-of-the-art Hopfield implementations.
note: A local, information-theoretic write rule rather than a global energy landscape; cleanly testable in KV/associative-memory models.
data_avail_evidence: The simulation data generated in this study can be reproduced using the code and parameters described in the Methods and Supplementary Information. The code is available at https://github.com/Priesemann-Group/Infomorphic_Networks. No external datasets were used in this study.
code_avail_evidence: The code to reproduce the results is available via the public GitHub repository https://github.com/Priesemann-Group/Infomorphic_Networks.

title: Oscillatory Phase Coding Emerges in Adaptive RNNs for Flexible Working Memory
authors: K. Lu et al. (S. Wu, H. Luo, F. Fang)
abstract: A bstract Oscillatory phase coding (OPC) is widely observed in neural systems and has been implicated in cognitive functions such as memory and sequence processing. However, its computational role and neural substrates remain largely unclear. Here, we studied OPC by training recurrent neural networks (RNNs) with adaptation to perform sequence working memory tasks with variable delays. After training, we found that OPC emerges in the RNN spontaneously: the memorized items recur at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with oscillation amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablation studies identified three key elements required for OPC: adaptation in neural dynamics, variable delay in memory retention, and flexibility in reading out information. Neuron-type analysis revealed the emergence of content and time cells in the trained RNN, and they process item identity and sequence order separately. Recurrent connectivity analysis revealed phase-organized connections among time cells and structured connections within digit-selective content-cell groups. Inspired by these findings, we proposed a neural circuit model which reproduces OPC through interactions between content units and an adaptive time ring. Together, this study reveals how OPC arises from network structures and task demands, offers insights into the implementation and computational mechanisms of OPC in biological systems, and inspires us to develop computational models for human-like cognitive functions.
approach: Trained adaptive recurrent neural networks on sequence working-memory tasks with variable delays, then ablated task/dynamic components, classified emergent neuron types, analysed recurrent connectivity, and built a reduced circuit model (content units plus an adaptive time ring).
finding: Oscillatory phase coding emerged without being built in: memorised items recurred at distinct phases of a shared rhythm, with amplitude encoding item identity and phase encoding serial order. Ablations showed three necessary ingredients — neural adaptation, variable retention delay, and flexible readout — and the trained networks spontaneously split into content cells and time cells with phase-organised connections among the latter. The reduced circuit reproduces the effect.
note: Preprint, not peer reviewed. A clean computational demonstration of identity and ordinal position being carried by orthogonal state variables — the Pillar 3 key/position separation in a biological-style substrate.

title: Naturalistic recall preserves temporal specificity despite cortical feature reorganization
authors: S. Peng et al. (B. Levine, B. R. Buchsbaum)
abstract: Although sensory input arrives in a largely continuous stream, recall is temporally compressed, discontinuous, and often structured as events. However, the temporal specificity of recall-related neural activity within events, and the separation and cortical organization of recalled features relative to perception, remain poorly characterized. We analyzed functional MRI data recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock. A data-driven alignment between viewing and recall data identified neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events and revealed information that distinguished moments within events, particularly in the association cortex. Features ranging from low-level visual to semantic information predicted recall reinstatement. However, differences in predictive performance among feature levels became smaller during recall, and their organization along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Thus, temporal specificity within events can be preserved despite substantial reorganization of feature representations across the cortex during recall.
approach: Re-analysed fMRI recorded during viewing and free recall of an episode of Sherlock, using data-driven alignment between viewing and recall to identify neural recapitulation of corresponding narrative events; feature levels from low-level visual to semantic were used to predict reinstatement and mapped along the cortical sensory-to-association gradient.
finding: Recall reinstated corresponding narrative events and carried information distinguishing moments within events, especially in association cortex. All feature levels predicted reinstatement, but differences in predictive performance among feature levels compressed during recall, and their organisation along the sensory-to-association gradient reversed relative to viewing. Within-event temporal specificity survives a substantial reorganisation of feature representations.
note: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Direct Sherlock-dataset result — the highest-priority item for the naturalistic-fMRI replication work; the gradient reversal is a concrete prediction for encoding-vs-recall alignment analyses.

title: The human hippocampus supports auditory coding and multisensory integration
authors: O. Raccah et al. (N. B. Turk-Browne)
abstract: Participants were exposed to multiple repetitions of short naturalistic movie clips, each presented in four formats: auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, and incongruent audiovisual. Using high-resolution fMRI, we measured univariate activation and multivariate representations across the longitudinal axis and subfields of the human hippocampus. Whereas univariate analyses detected only visual responses, multivariate analyses revealed robust representations of both auditory and visual scenes; posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli, and anterior hippocampus showed crossmodal decoding driven by the right hemisphere.
approach: High-resolution fMRI while participants saw repeated short naturalistic movie clips in four formats — auditory-only, visual-only, congruent audiovisual, incongruent audiovisual — measuring univariate activation and multivariate representations along the longitudinal axis and across hippocampal subfields, plus whole-brain searchlight analyses.
finding: Univariate analyses detected only visual responses, with no auditory activation and no congruent-stimulus benefit, but multivariate patterns robustly represented both auditory and visual scenes. Posterior hippocampus showed enhanced pattern similarity for congruent stimuli (left-lateralised), while anterior hippocampus supported crossmodal decoding of the same clip across modalities (right-lateralised), implying a more abstract code. Cortical multisensory regions showed parallel effects.
note: Naturalistic movie-clip paradigm; a useful control for anyone running RSA/ISC on audiovisual narratives — univariate nulls can coexist with strong multivariate coding.
data_avail_evidence: The raw and preprocessed fMRI data are available on OpenNeuro (https://doi.org/10.18112/openneuro.ds008849.v1.0.0). The task code is publicly available at https://github.com/omriraccah/multimem_fMRI_expt and the analysis code at https://github.com/omriraccah/multimem_fMRI_analysis and via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22150287. The source data underlying the figures are available on OSF
code_avail_evidence: The raw and preprocessed fMRI data are available on OpenNeuro (https://doi.org/10.18112/openneuro.ds008849.v1.0.0). The task code is publicly available at https://github.com/omriraccah/multimem_fMRI_expt and the analysis code at https://github.com/omriraccah/multimem_fMRI_analysis and via Zenodo at https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22150287. The source data underlying the figures are available on OSF

title: Gaze reinstatement during working memory for natural scenes
abstract: The information we hold in mind with working memory (WM) may propagate beyond the cortex and out to the peripheral motor system. For instance, directionally biased hand and eye movements can express simple visuo-spatial features during WM maintenance. If such sensorimotor inflections are a form of WM representation, they may also express more detailed and task-adaptive information about WM content. Here, we ask whether gaze patterns carry item-specific detail about complex stimuli held in mind, and whether gaze during WM maintenance adapts to upcoming behavioral demands. To do this, we tracked male and female human eye movements during WM for naturalistic images, and we manipulated which image properties were most task-relevant (visual or semantic). In two experiments, we found that the eyes moved in item-specific spatiotemporal sequences during WM maintenance. Delay period gaze patterns retraced the scanpaths from stimulus encoding, echoing the ‘gaze reinstatement’ that has been observed during long-term memory retrieval. Therefore, gaze patterns during WM may reinstate visual encoding processes for maintenance. We also used time-resolved representational similarity analyses, guided by convolutional neural network modeling, to test the specificity of WM gaze patterns across a trial. We found that gaze representations were more distinct when the task prioritized visual detail, and they also ramped up in anticipation of the WM probe. Therefore, oculomotor WM signals are malleable to when and how the content will be used. WM may recruit the most primary structures in sensorimotor processing, where eye movements reflect flexible and future-oriented WM content information. Significance Statement The eyes are an outwardly accessible extension of the brain. They filter sensory input and enact motor output, but may also offer a rich window into underlying cognition. For instance, pupil dilation can reflect changing cognitive load, and biased eye movements can reflect basic spatial information about content held in mind with working memory (WM). WM is a critical neuro-cognitive function, but its physiological bases remain under debate. Here, we show that during WM the eyes can move in intricate patterns that read out the complex, real-world stimuli held in mind. This work shows how cognitive states influence oculomotor functions, and also advances theories of WM maintenance to include the most basic structures in sensorimotor processing.
approach: Two experiments tracked eye movements while human participants held naturalistic images in working memory, varying whether visual or semantic image properties were task-relevant; time-resolved representational similarity analysis guided by CNN modelling tested the specificity of delay-period gaze patterns.
finding: Delay-period gaze moved in item-specific spatiotemporal sequences that retraced encoding scanpaths — gaze reinstatement during maintenance, previously described only for long-term retrieval. Gaze representations were more distinct when visual detail was prioritised and ramped up in anticipation of the memory probe, so the oculomotor signal is both content-specific and tuned to when and how the content will be used.
note: Naturalistic images, controlled trial-based WM design. Extends cortical reinstatement to the peripheral motor system.

title: Amnesia Induced by Suppressing the Focus of Internal Attention
authors: A. Satish et al. (J. C. Hulbert, M. C. Anderson)
abstract: Our thoughts can recede as we direct attention to the external world. This experience may reflect the suppression of thoughts about past events, future worries, or stray ideas that could otherwise disrupt focus. Such thoughts may arise spontaneously from replay mechanisms supported by the episodic memory system; hence, sustaining external focus may require suppressing these systems to stop internal distraction. Here, periods of high external focus disrupted diverse episodic content activated near in time, inducing an 'amnesic shadow'. This shadow occurred for both novel content and already formed memories and exhibited key markers of active suppression: forgetting beyond expectations from time alone, which generalised to an alternative reminder. External attention therefore automatically engages an active suppression mechanism that appears to broadly inhibit cognitive systems supporting the emergence of distracting thoughts. The findings raise the possibility that people may naturally gravitate toward activities demanding external attention, unwittingly, to regulate unwanted thoughts.
approach: Behavioural experiments contrasting periods of high versus low external attentional focus and measuring subsequent memory for episodic content activated near in time, with an alternative-reminder test to distinguish passive decay from active suppression.
finding: High external focus disrupted diverse episodic content activated nearby in time, producing an 'amnesic shadow' for both novel content and already-formed memories. Forgetting exceeded what time alone predicts and generalised to an alternative reminder — the signature of active suppression rather than decay. External attention thus automatically engages a broad inhibition of the systems that generate distracting internal content, including replay-supported episodic retrieval.
note: Preprint, not peer reviewed. Mechanistically relevant to Pillar 1 (attention-contingent retention/forgetting), but the human-behaviour design cannot isolate a replay mechanism — flag as an inference, not a measurement.

title: In-group neural alignment serves as a biomarker of social identity
abstract: In this study, we propose a perspective on neural synchronization. Beyond reflecting shared understanding between individuals, we suggest it serves as a biological marker of social homogeneity. We examined fMRI neural responses of 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives. While explicit measures of emotional response, agreement, and engagement showed no significant differences in within-group variance, religious participants—representing a tighter social structure—exhibited significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and brain networks. Remarkably, synchrony values predicted religious orientation with an accuracy of up to 92%. We conclude that a community’s homogeneous social structure drives pervasive neural alignment, positioning neural synchrony as a potential signature of group cohesion beyond explicit behavioral measures.
approach: fMRI from 42 participants (21 religious, 21 secular) watching neutral and religion-relevant video narratives; inter-subject neural synchrony was computed within groups across content types and brain networks and compared with explicit ratings of emotion, agreement and engagement.
finding: Explicit measures showed no within-group variance differences, yet the tighter-structured religious group showed significantly higher in-group neural synchrony across all content types and networks, and synchrony predicted religious orientation with up to 92% accuracy. Neural alignment indexes social homogeneity even when behaviour does not.
note: Naturalistic video paradigm with an ISC measure — directly actionable for the naturalistic-fMRI replication work: ISC carries group structure, not just shared stimulus understanding.

title: When Model Complexity Matters in Cross-Subject Naturalistic fMRI Prediction
abstract: Abstract: Increasingly complex neural models predict blood-oxygen-level-dependent (BOLD) responses to naturalistic stimuli, but the predictive value of this added complexity remains unclear. We ask when pretrained stimulus representations help and how much downstream complexity is needed, with and without recent measured BOLD history. We compare linear diagnostic references and nonlinear predictors across HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10 subjects), and Algonauts 2025 (4 subjects). Under a shared offline protocol, models are fitted on training subjects and evaluated on held-out subjects viewing largely familiar stimuli, without refitting. Pretrained visual features generally improve prediction over raw pixels; for linear autoregression, this advantage becomes more pronounced over longer rollouts (recursive predictions without additional measured BOLD). Measured BOLD history provides substantial gains that generally diminish {as rollouts lengthen}. Nonlinear stimulus-only predictors can improve on linear readouts, whereas linear autoregression provides a strong history-conditioned baseline. Controls examine context length, regularization, fitting procedures, and model capacity. Regional response consistency across subjects is associated with held-out prediction accuracy, while less consistent regions tend to gain more from measured history. In paired simulations with fixed linear neural dynamics, slower hemodynamic responses generally sustain high temporal prediction correlations over longer rollouts, illustrating how the observation process can contribute to predictive persistence. Together, these findings support evaluating stimulus representations and downstream complexity separately, using history-conditioned linear prediction as a diagnostic reference under matched inputs and measurement availability.
approach: Shared offline cross-subject protocol (fit on training subjects, evaluate held-out subjects without refitting) across HCP movie fMRI (154 subjects), BOLD Moments (10) and Algonauts 2025 (4), comparing raw pixels vs pretrained features, linear vs nonlinear downstream predictors, and stimulus-only, history-only and history-conditioned inputs; plus controlled audiovisual simulations with an explicit hemodynamic model.
finding: Measured BOLD history gives substantial gains that diminish as rollouts lengthen; nonlinear stimulus-only models can beat linear readouts, but linear autoregression is a strong history-conditioned baseline. Regional cross-subject response consistency predicts held-out accuracy, and less consistent regions gain more from measured history. Simulations show slower hemodynamic responses alone sustain high temporal prediction correlations over longer rollouts — part of the apparent 'memory' is the measurement process.
note: arXiv preprint posted 11-02, one day before this run's window and missed by the 11-04 harvest — recovered here with the date stated. Methodological controls (matched inputs, history-conditioned linear reference, hemodynamic confound) are directly usable in split-half reliability analyses of ds005658.

title: Brain Decoding from a Deep Neural Network of Visual Memory Reveals the Maturation Trajectory of Memory Systems across Ages 3-7
authors: X. Guo et al. (Y. C. Leong, W. A. Bainbridge)
abstract: Memories from the first four years of life are largely inaccessible by adulthood, yet these early experiences profoundly shape cognition throughout development. Understanding this phenomenon of infantile amnesia is critical for revealing the mechanisms of early memory development. Here, we developed a new content-based behavioral measure of memory that quantifies how closely children's memory patterns resemble those of adults, which we term the memory maturation score. Using a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood, we trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked brain activity to predict adult's propensity to remember each movie snippet, estimated by ResMem, a deep neural network trained to predict visual memorability. We then applied the model to each child's brain activity while viewing the same movie to assess their memory maturation (i.e., cross-decodability from adult patterns). Children exhibited adult-like neural patterns of memory around age 4, extending prior behavioral findings. Structural analyses showed that the volume of the left posterior hippocampus, but not age or total brain volume, significantly predicted children's memory maturation. Memory maturation around age 4 thus likely reflects age-related neural development of hippocampal memory systems, rather than an age increase itself. Functional searchlight analyses revealed a trajectory of memory maturation: the inferior temporal gyrus reflected mature memory-related processing from age 3 onward, the left posterior hippocampus by age 5, and higher-order regions involved in social-affective processing and multimodal integration by age 7. Together, these findings suggest that hippocampal maturation between ages 3 and 5 drives the maturation of memory patterns.
approach: Used a movie-watching fMRI dataset spanning age 3 to adulthood; trained a cross-validated model on adults' movie-evoked activity to predict ResMem (a DNN memorability estimate) for each clip, then applied it to each child's activity while viewing the same movie to derive a 'memory maturation score', followed by structural and searchlight analyses.
finding: Children showed adult-like neural memory patterns around age 4. Left posterior hippocampal volume — not chronological age or total brain volume — predicted the maturation score, and searchlight analyses traced a sequence: inferior temporal gyrus mature from age 3, left posterior hippocampus by 5, higher-order social-affective and multimodal regions by 7.
note: Preprint, not peer reviewed; naturalistic movie paradigm. Cross-decodability from an adult model is an indirect measure of memory maturation, and the structural result is correlational.
